<div class="page-shell">

<header class="masthead">
  <div class="eyebrow">WebR practical</div>
  <h1>Interaction terms in regression</h1>
  <p>Fit models where the effect of one predictor depends on another predictor, then translate the coefficient table into group-specific slopes.</p>
</header>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Overview</h2>

In an additive model, each predictor has its own contribution:

```r
lm(outcome ~ x + z, data = my_data)
```

That model assumes the slope of <code>x</code> is the same at every value or level of <code>z</code>. An interaction model relaxes that assumption:

```r
lm(outcome ~ x * z, data = my_data)
```

The shorthand <code>x * z</code> expands to <code>x + z + x:z</code>. The new <code>x:z</code> term is the interaction.

In this practical you will:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li>Fit a continuous by binary categorical interaction.</li>
  <li>Use a slope table to decode the reference and non-reference groups.</li>
  <li>Extend the same idea to a three-level categorical variable.</li>
  <li>Fit a continuous by continuous interaction and explain why centering helps.</li>
</ul>

After answering the questions, <strong>your completion code will be revealed.</strong>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 1</div>
  <p>Which R formula fits an interaction between <code>BMI</code> and <code>BPmeds</code>?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="a"><code>lm(sysBP ~ BMI + BPmeds, data = bp_binary)</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="b"><code>lm(sysBP ~ BMI * BPmeds, data = bp_binary)</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="c"><code>lm(BMI ~ sysBP * BPmeds, data = bp_binary)</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The star asks R for both main effects and the interaction term." data-incorrect="Not quite. The outcome goes on the left, and BMI * BPmeds puts the interaction on the right."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>The blood pressure question</h2>

We will use small teaching datasets about systolic blood pressure.

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><code>sysBP</code>: systolic blood pressure.</li>
  <li><code>BMI</code>: body mass index.</li>
  <li><code>BPmeds</code>: whether the person takes blood pressure medication.</li>
  <li><code>med_group</code>: a three-level medication group.</li>
  <li><code>age</code>: age in years.</li>
</ul>

The scientific question is not just "Does BMI predict systolic BP?" It is: <strong>does the BMI slope change across medication status, medication group, or age?</strong>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: create the teaching datasets</h3>

```{webr-r}
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

bmi_values <- c(22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 37)

bp_binary <- data.frame(
  BMI = rep(bmi_values, times = 2),
  BPmeds = factor(
    rep(c("No_meds", "On_meds"), each = length(bmi_values)),
    levels = c("No_meds", "On_meds")
  )
)

bp_binary$sysBP <- with(
  bp_binary,
  ifelse(BPmeds == "No_meds",
         87.64 + 1.70 * BMI,
         144.75 + 0.70 * BMI)
)

bp_poly <- data.frame(
  BMI = rep(bmi_values, times = 3),
  med_group = factor(
    rep(c("No_meds", "ACE", "Beta_blocker"), each = length(bmi_values)),
    levels = c("No_meds", "ACE", "Beta_blocker")
  )
)

bp_poly$sysBP <- with(
  bp_poly,
  ifelse(med_group == "No_meds",
         87.64 + 1.70 * BMI,
         ifelse(med_group == "ACE",
                125.00 + 0.95 * BMI,
                145.00 + 0.60 * BMI))
)

bp_age <- expand.grid(
  BMI = c(24, 27, 30, 33, 36),
  age = c(50, 60, 70)
)

bp_age$BMI_c <- bp_age$BMI - 30
bp_age$age_c <- bp_age$age - 60
bp_age$sysBP <- with(
  bp_age,
  130 + 1.20 * BMI_c + 0.60 * age_c + 0.04 * BMI_c * age_c
)

head(bp_binary)
```

</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Binary categorical moderator</h2>

First compare two models:

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Model</th><th>Formula</th><th>What it allows</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Additive</td><td><code>sysBP ~ BMI + BPmeds</code></td><td>Two lines with different intercepts but the same BMI slope.</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Interaction</td><td><code>sysBP ~ BMI * BPmeds</code></td><td>Two lines, where medication status can change the BMI slope.</td></tr>
</table>

If the interaction is useful, the fitted lines are not parallel. The effect of BMI depends on whether the person is on medication.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: plot the binary groups</h3>

```{webr-r}
ggplot(bp_binary, aes(x = BMI, y = sysBP, color = BPmeds)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2f5f98", "#b83b5e")) +
  labs(
    x = "BMI",
    y = "Systolic BP",
    color = "Medication"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 2</div>
  <p>In the plot, what visual pattern suggests an interaction?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="a">The two fitted lines have different slopes.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="b">The two groups have exactly the same fitted line.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="c">The outcome variable is on the x-axis.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Different slopes mean the BMI effect changes by medication status." data-incorrect="Not quite. For a continuous by categorical interaction, look for non-parallel fitted lines."></div>
</div>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit additive and interaction models</h3>

```{webr-r}
mod_binary_add <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI + BPmeds, data = bp_binary)
mod_binary_int <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI * BPmeds, data = bp_binary)

round(coef(mod_binary_add), 2)
round(coef(mod_binary_int), 2)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 3</div>
  <p>What does <code>BMI * BPmeds</code> expand to in an R formula?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="a"><code>BMI:BPmeds</code> only</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="b"><code>BMI + BPmeds</code> only</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="c"><code>BMI + BPmeds + BMI:BPmeds</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The star keeps both main effects and adds the interaction." data-incorrect="Not quite. In R, the star is shorthand for both main effects plus the colon interaction."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Read the binary interaction table</h2>

For the interaction model, rounded coefficients are:

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Term</th><th>Estimate</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">(Intercept)</span></td><td>87.64</td><td>Intercept for the reference group, <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BMI</span></td><td>1.70</td><td>BMI slope for the reference group.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BPmedsOn_meds</span></td><td>57.11</td><td>How much the <code>On_meds</code> intercept differs from the reference intercept.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BMI:BPmedsOn_meds</span></td><td>-1.00</td><td>How much the <code>On_meds</code> BMI slope differs from the reference slope.</td></tr>
</table>

The key move is to build a small slope table:

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>BMI slope</th></tr>
  <tr><td><code>No_meds</code> reference</td><td>87.64</td><td>1.70</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>On_meds</code></td><td>87.64 + 57.11 = <strong>144.75</strong></td><td>1.70 + (-1.00) = <strong>0.70</strong></td></tr>
</table>

The reference group's slope is the plain <code>BMI</code> row. The non-reference group's slope is the plain <code>BMI</code> row plus its interaction row.

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 4</div>
  <p>In the binary interaction model, which coefficient gives the BMI slope for the reference group <code>No_meds</code>?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="a"><code>BMI</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="b"><code>BPmedsOn_meds</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="c"><code>BMI:BPmedsOn_meds</code> by itself</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The plain BMI row is the BMI slope for the reference group." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction row is an adjustment to the reference slope, not the full slope by itself."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 5</div>
  <p>What is the BMI slope for the <code>On_meds</code> group?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="a"><code>-1.00</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="b"><code>1.70 + (-1.00) = 0.70</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="c"><code>87.64 + 57.11 = 144.75</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Add the BMI row and the BMI:BPmedsOn_meds row." data-incorrect="Not quite. The interaction term is the difference from the reference BMI slope."></div>
</div>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the binary interaction yourself</h3>

Replace each <code>____</code>, then run the cell.

```{webr-r}
my_binary_model <- lm(____ ~ ____ * ____, data = bp_binary)
round(coef(my_binary_model), 2)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
my_binary_model <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI * BPmeds, data = bp_binary)
round(coef(my_binary_model), 2)
```

</details>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Predict from the binary interaction</h2>

For a person on medication, use the <code>On_meds</code> row from the slope table:

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} = 144.75 + 0.70 \times \text{BMI}
$$

</div>

For a person not on medication, use the reference row:

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} = 87.64 + 1.70 \times \text{BMI}
$$

</div>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 6</div>
  <p>Using the binary interaction table, what is the predicted systolic BP for someone on medication with BMI = 30?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="a"><code>87.64 + 1.70 * 30 = 138.64</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="b"><code>144.75 + 0.70 * 30 = 165.75</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="c"><code>57.11 + (-1.00) * 30 = 27.11</code></label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Use the intercept and BMI slope for the On_meds row." data-incorrect="Not quite. First move to the On_meds row of the slope table, then plug in BMI = 30."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Polytomous categorical moderator</h2>

Now replace the binary medication variable with a three-level medication group:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><code>No_meds</code>, the reference group.</li>
  <li><code>ACE</code>, a non-reference group.</li>
  <li><code>Beta_blocker</code>, another non-reference group.</li>
</ul>

With a three-level categorical variable, R creates two dummy variables because one group is the reference. The interaction model therefore creates two interaction rows: one slope adjustment for <code>ACE</code> and one slope adjustment for <code>Beta_blocker</code>.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the polytomous interaction</h3>

```{webr-r}
ggplot(bp_poly, aes(x = BMI, y = sysBP, color = med_group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2f5f98", "#287a4d", "#b83b5e")) +
  labs(
    x = "BMI",
    y = "Systolic BP",
    color = "Medication group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

mod_poly_int <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI * med_group, data = bp_poly)
round(coef(mod_poly_int), 2)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 7</div>
  <p>With three medication groups and <code>No_meds</code> as the reference, how many BMI interaction rows does R create?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="a">One, because there is only one BMI variable.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="b">Two, one for each non-reference medication group.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="c">Three, one for every medication group including the reference.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. A three-level factor has two non-reference levels, so there are two slope adjustments." data-incorrect="Not quite. The reference group is represented by the intercept and plain BMI row, so it does not get its own dummy row."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Read the three-level interaction table</h2>

Rounded coefficients from <code>lm(sysBP ~ BMI * med_group)</code> are:

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Term</th><th>Estimate</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">(Intercept)</span></td><td>87.64</td><td>Intercept for <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BMI</span></td><td>1.70</td><td>BMI slope for <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">med_groupACE</span></td><td>37.36</td><td>ACE intercept difference from <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">med_groupBeta_blocker</span></td><td>57.36</td><td>Beta blocker intercept difference from <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BMI:med_groupACE</span></td><td>-0.75</td><td>ACE BMI slope difference from <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="term-chip">BMI:med_groupBeta_blocker</span></td><td>-1.10</td><td>Beta blocker BMI slope difference from <code>No_meds</code>.</td></tr>
</table>

The same reference-plus-adjustment logic applies, but now there is one adjustment per non-reference level:

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Medication group</th><th>Intercept</th><th>BMI slope</th></tr>
  <tr><td><code>No_meds</code> reference</td><td>87.64</td><td>1.70</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>ACE</code></td><td>87.64 + 37.36 = <strong>125.00</strong></td><td>1.70 + (-0.75) = <strong>0.95</strong></td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>Beta_blocker</code></td><td>87.64 + 57.36 = <strong>145.00</strong></td><td>1.70 + (-1.10) = <strong>0.60</strong></td></tr>
</table>

</section>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Continuous moderator</h2>

Interactions are not only for groups. A continuous predictor can also modify a slope.

Here the question is: <strong>does the BMI slope change with age?</strong>

Before fitting the interaction, we center the predictors:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><code>BMI_c = BMI - 30</code>, so <code>BMI_c = 0</code> means BMI 30.</li>
  <li><code>age_c = age - 60</code>, so <code>age_c = 0</code> means age 60.</li>
</ul>

Centering is not required for the model to fit, but it makes the lower-order terms easier to read.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the continuous by continuous interaction</h3>

```{webr-r}
ggplot(bp_age, aes(x = BMI, y = sysBP, color = factor(age))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2f5f98", "#287a4d", "#b83b5e")) +
  labs(
    x = "BMI",
    y = "Systolic BP",
    color = "Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

mod_age_int <- lm(sysBP ~ BMI_c * age_c, data = bp_age)
round(coef(mod_age_int), 2)
```

</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Read the continuous interaction</h2>

The fitted equation is:

<div class="formula-panel">

$$
\widehat{\text{sysBP}} =
130 + 1.20 \times \text{BMI_c} + 0.60 \times \text{age_c}
+ 0.04 \times (\text{BMI_c} \times \text{age_c})
$$

</div>

For a continuous moderator, the slope table is no longer "reference group versus non-reference group." Instead, choose meaningful values of the moderator and plug them into the slope formula.

<table class="coef-table">
  <tr><th>Age</th><th><code>age_c</code></th><th>BMI slope formula</th><th>BMI slope</th></tr>
  <tr><td>50</td><td>-10</td><td>1.20 + 0.04 x (-10)</td><td><strong>0.80</strong></td></tr>
  <tr><td>60</td><td>0</td><td>1.20 + 0.04 x 0</td><td><strong>1.20</strong></td></tr>
  <tr><td>70</td><td>10</td><td>1.20 + 0.04 x 10</td><td><strong>1.60</strong></td></tr>
</table>

So the plain <code>BMI_c</code> coefficient is the BMI slope when <code>age_c = 0</code>. Because we centered age at 60, that means the BMI slope at age 60.

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">

<section class="panel">

<h2>What to remember</h2>

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><code>x * z</code> means <code>x + z + x:z</code>.</li>
  <li>With a binary categorical moderator, the reference slope is the plain <code>x</code> row and the other slope is <code>x</code> plus the interaction row.</li>
  <li>With a polytomous categorical moderator, each non-reference level gets its own slope adjustment.</li>
  <li>With a continuous moderator, calculate the <code>x</code> slope at meaningful moderator values.</li>
  <li>Center continuous variables when zero is not meaningful.</li>
</ul>

</section>

<script>
const COMPLETION_CODE = "INTXBP55";
const COMPLETION_REQUIRED = 10;

function updateCompletion() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".practice");
  const correct = document.querySelectorAll(".practice.is-correct").length;
  const total = cards.length;
  const progress = document.getElementById("code-progress");
  const box = document.getElementById("code-box");
  const value = document.getElementById("code-value");

  if (progress) {
    progress.textContent = correct + " of " + total + " correct (need at least " + COMPLETION_REQUIRED + ")";
  }

  if (box && value) {
    if (correct >= COMPLETION_REQUIRED) {
      value.textContent = COMPLETION_CODE;
      box.style.display = "block";
    } else {
      box.style.display = "none";
    }
  }
}

document.querySelectorAll(".practice").forEach((card) => {
  const button = card.querySelector("button");
  const feedback = card.querySelector(".practice-feedback");
  const answer = card.dataset.answer;

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const selected = card.querySelector("input[type='radio']:checked");
    card.classList.remove("is-correct", "is-incorrect");
    card.querySelectorAll("label").forEach((label) => {
      label.classList.remove("correct-choice", "incorrect-choice");
    });

    if (!selected) {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      feedback.textContent = "Choose an answer first, then check it.";
      updateCompletion();
      return;
    }

    const selectedLabel = selected.closest("label");
    const correctInput = card.querySelector(`input[value="${answer}"]`);
    const correctLabel = correctInput ? correctInput.closest("label") : null;

    if (selected.value === answer) {
      card.classList.add("is-correct");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.correct;
    } else {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("incorrect-choice");
      if (correctLabel) correctLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.incorrect;
    }

    updateCompletion();
  });
});

updateCompletion();
</script>
